script: Punished for over-performing, so I did the bare minimum before leaving.... Part 1: I worked remotely for an auto parts company for almost four years, finally getting a promotion after the company merged with another. The vibe was good, the team was tight, and my performance was on fire. I was the one who always hit my numbers before anyone else, and that made me feel like the MVP of the office. The new owner was a local legend who sold classic parts from Model T to muscle cars, and they had a huge online reach. The company was supposed to be a dream, but the tech side was a nightmare. They bought a new sales/parts/service program that promised to sync inventory and accounting. It turned into a circus: 10 pieces listed in one program, none in another, a vendor due payment in one sheet, and nothing owed in another. The only person who knew what was happening was the manager who left with a fat severance. The chaos spread. Customers started complaining, vendors pulled back, and I, as a case manager, was on the front line, juggling calls and trying to keep people happy. The turnover was high, the company was teetering on bankruptcy, and BAP—Big Auto Parts—stepped in. They paid vendors, fixed accounts, and cut 60% of staff. It was brutal, but the business survived. Six months after the merger, I got promoted to Customer Operations Specialist. My new role was to research issues and pass them to Lucy, who would talk to customers about solutions. In three weeks, Lucy decided she didn't fit, leaving a hole that I had to fill. I was already used to making calls, so I handled both research and calls. It was a win, and my supervisor saw it, so I got a raise. I was making good money doing something I liked, and I felt like the queen of the department. The company grew, and the ticket system became a nightmare. Hundreds of irrelevant tickets would pop up at random times, and I noticed patterns. I would call out the issues to my supervisor so someone higher could fix the underlying problem. I was the only one who could see the whole picture, and the rest of the team was stuck in their lanes. I was asked to cross-train into other areas, and I nailed it. I did other people's jobs better than they did. It was a combo of my drive to succeed and their willingness to do the bare minimum. I was a step ahead of everyone, and that made me feel untouchable. The point system was a beast. It tracked tickets, time, and follow-ups. My metrics were sky-high; I hit the weekly bonus every week, earning $2.50 more per hour. I was over $20 an hour for most of the year, and that was a sweet spot. I was required to make 200 calls and 2400 points, but I did 300-500 calls and nearly 7000 points. I was the star performer, and the bonus made me feel invincible. In college, I studied video production, but I had no idea I'd become a ticket wizard. I was traveling to the corporate office, making friends, and even the owners knew me by name. My wife, who worked for the sheriff, emailed me about a media opening. I applied, went through a three-month process, and got a call from the sheriff himself saying he was excited I applied. I was on a high, but my supervisor had been giving me a hard time. He told me my numbers were too high, that no one else made as many points, and that changes were coming. I was about to start at the sheriff's office when he told me the new point system would slash my points to 1800 from 7000, dropping me below the bonus threshold. He said, "That's what the company wants to do." I was shocked. My bonus had put me over $20 an hour, and the new job would pay even more. I was ready to hand in my two weeks' notice.
